baseline_reason: Every dropped target counted here predates the gate and each needs its own decision, so --strict fails on a rise rather than demanding zero. Lower this number whenever a case file regains a backend; the gate fails on a drop too, so an improvement cannot be silently spent. The unit is one (case, target) pair, never (file, target): a sequence-style file states one scenario across prep/act/verify cases, so a backend dropped from only the verifying case still runs every step that cannot fail and silently skips the assertion, and a union over the file would report that backend as covered. What this gate exists to catch is the failure mode that hid two real bugs: a backend that cannot pass a case is normally just deleted from that case's `targets`, which turns a divergence into an omission no reviewer can see. integ/unix/mv/empty_dir.json had dropbox and dropbox-root removed for a folder-conflict divergence, and s3/gridfs removed because a directory rename was unimplemented on both -- neither omission said so anywhere. A large share of the remaining count is the tier2/unicode/escape family, whose cases pin text-processing behavior that cannot vary by backend and so run on the core four; those are excusable in bulk once someone confirms that file by file, which is exactly the decision this gate is meant to force rather than assume. Lowered 2295 -> 2289 when cmp/{n,b,i}.json landed: the gate compares each case against its directory's MODAL target set, and cmp's mode was decided by a 2-vs-2 tie broken toward the larger set, so the two fixture-reading cases (basic.json, which only reads /data/a.txt) set the expectation and the two write-seeding ones (l.json, s.json) each reported a 3-target omission. The new cases seed the same way l.json does -- `mkdir -p` plus `printf >` -- which databricks, databricks-prefix and sharepoint-prefix cannot serve, so they carry l.json's list and the write-seeding shape is now the majority. Those 6 pairs are a real capability limit rather than a parked divergence: cmp itself runs on all 22 (basic.json proves it), only the seeding does not. Nothing was narrowed to make a case pass. Raised 2289 -> 2290 when stat/c.json gained stat_mount_root_names_the_operand: the modal set for integ/unix/stat/ includes statvfs, whose one mount is /vfs, and every case in c.json states its path as the literal /data, so all four of them drop it. The new case is the fourth of that shape rather than a new kind of omission, and no coverage is parked: statvfs mounts ram, and ram is one of the 22 targets the new case does name, so the question it asks is answered for that backend at /data. Raised 2290 -> 2350 when session/modes.json gained the twelve link-write cases that pin the namespace table against a session's read grant: a session case can only run on a target that declares the session it names, and `reader` is declared on ram and disk only while `root_ro` is declared on ram-root only, so the six /data cases each drop that directory's modal gridfs/redis/s3/s3-prefix and the six root cases additionally drop disk and ram. That is the shape of every case already in the file, including the five sess_root_* ones the new root cases sit beside; nothing was narrowed to make a case pass, and no backend question is parked, since a session grant is namespace state that the mount's backend never sees. Then lowered 2350 -> 2226 by three more cases in the same file, and the drop is a MODAL-SET FLIP, not coverage regained: this measure scores each case against its own directory's most common target set, and session/ had so few ram+disk cases that the fuller list was modal, so every ram+disk case was counted as dropping it. The three new /ro cases tip ram+disk into being modal, whereupon the twenty cases naming it drop nothing and only the eleven ram-root ones drop two each. Not one case gained a backend, so do not read 2226 as more coverage than 2350 -- it is the same coverage measured against a different modal set, locked in because the gate fails on a drop as loudly as on a rise. The three cases themselves park no question: they pin that a read-only MOUNT still takes a symlink while still refusing the backend write, which is a namespace-plane fact the mount's backend never sees, and integ/resources/<svc>/sym.json already pins it above postgres, mongodb, chroma and qdrant.

files.integ/unix/gzip/f.json: Same list as gzip/k.json, the sibling that pins -k. -f only decides whether an existing archive is overwritten, which every backend in that list already exercises through the write primitive.
files.integ/unix/ls/t.json: -t sorts on mtime, so the case has to set three distinct mtimes with touch -d first; the list is touch/d.json's, the backends that support setting one.
files.integ/secrets/env.json: Two workspaces on purpose: secrets-env declares live sources and secrets-dead declares DEAD on a source whose fetch always fails, so each case is meaningful on exactly one of them -- a dead-source case has nothing to prove where the fetch succeeds, and a fetch case cannot pass where it cannot. No backend question is parked: both targets mount the same ram resource, and the split is the env declaration, which no mount sees.
files.integ/bash/test/filepair.json: -nt/-ot compare two mtimes, so the case has to set a distinct one with touch -d first; the list is touch/d.json's, the backends that support setting one.
files.integ/bash/exec/path.json: Every case seeds a script with `printf >` and then runs it, and databricks, databricks-prefix and sharepoint-prefix cannot serve that seeding (the same three cmp/l.json omits for the same reason), so the file has always carried the 19-target list. It only reads as a gap because descriptors.json's two cases, which write nothing since the fd-3 refusal happens before any write, joined redirect.json's six and tipped the directory's modal set to 22. Nothing was narrowed; exec itself is proved on all 22 by the other two files.

integ/bash/assign/export_attr.json :: cd.hf: hf holds no empty directory: the service refuses a directory marker client-side (create_dir=false, probed on opendal 0.47.1), so mkdir is a no-op and a directory exists exactly while it holds a key. This case has to cd into a directory it just made and never keyed, so on hf the cd fails and PWD/OLDPWD never take the values being asserted. The script_* monty twins in this same file run on ram-commands, so a per-command profile script is still judged on the modal target and only the second engine rides the narrower one.

integ/bash/command/findexec.json :: find.gdrive: This backend's find core accepts the mtime window for signature parity and applies nothing: core/object_store/find.py (s3, gridfs, hf) and core/gdrive/find.py (matching onedrive and sharepoint) both document -mtime as a deliberate no-op because their synthetic directories carry no mtime. -newermt folds into that same window, so a future date matches everything there where GNU matches nothing. The divergence predates -newermt and is a parked backend question, not a shell one; the parse-error and missing-reference siblings still run on every backend.
